claims.text: About five centuries before Christ a vampire calling itself the Dagda claimed Ireland, made no childer, and forced the few other Cainites there to submit or die; some call it a Ventrue childe of Mithras.

In the second century before Christ a Brujah blood witch remembered as the Morrigan fled war in Greece to Ireland; after long fighting the two split the island north and south and met twice a year to settle disputes.
Druids driven from Gaul later hunted the lesser vampires and slew the Morrigan, so the Dagda killed most of them and Embraced three as childer.
As the Dagda slept more, three druid childer known as the Lords of Connacht ran the domain and tested newcomers’ loyalty.
They never forgave the murder of their fellow druids, and about fifty years after Christ’s death they ambushed and slew their sire while it hunted.
One of them is said to have taken the Dagda’s soul along with its blood.

title: The clans in the Isles
summary: Where the clans stand in the Fiefs of Avalon.

claims.text: Only the Holy Roman Empire outranks the Isles as a Ventrue stronghold in the princes’ wars, and every Ventrue there pays homage to Mithras, lord of London.
Many Toreador look to the French courts, among them Melusine d’Anjou, the self-styled Queen of Winchester and Mithras’ rival.
Lucius of the Cainite Heresy watches over the Heresy’s interests in Lincoln, and Mithras detests the Lasombra, so few of them stay.
Mithras welcomes the Assamites as old allies; a small coterie under the vizier Hassan of the Bloody Hand stays in Bristol as guests.

title: The Tremere in the Isles
summary: The Low Clan the Isles despise most.

claims.text: Mithras openly loathes the Tremere, which makes rival Melusine’s alliance with them all the more bitter.
The Usurpers keep chantries in County Clare and in Durham and have agents in Oxford and Cambridge seeking recruits and hidden Hermetic magi.
Several Hermetic chantries in the Isles are marked for plunder, though the Massasa War burns less fiercely here than in eastern Europe.

title: Matthew of Lindisfarne
summary: Perhaps the only Salubri in the Isles.

claims.text: Matthew is a warrior turned ascetic whose writings on calming the Beast are prized by followers of the Road of Heaven.
A cell of the shadow Inquisition at Lindisfarne has no idea the gentle old monk is Cainite, and Matthew helps those inquisitors whenever possible.
Mithras respects Matthew’s reputation, which also shields the Salubri from Tremere killers.
The Ravnos of the Isles travel the roads as peddlers, workmen, thieves and entertainers, and seem to be very few.
These western Ravnos have little to do with their kin in the East, keep to themselves and stay out of the War of Princes.

title: Haunted places of the Isles
summary: Ghost tales told across Britain and Ireland.

claims.text: A castle lies beneath Lough Gur, where the sorcerer Gerald Desmond rises every seven years on a silver-shod white horse; whoever seizes the rein may claim the grimoires.
Cornish wreckers drowned in storms are said to walk on stormy nights hunting the treasure hidden in their caves, which turns to salt water unless a priest blesses it.
Bramber Castle in Sussex is said to hold the ghosts of three de Braose children starved by King John and of Lady Maud de Hurst, murdered in 1210.

title: Fae and demons in Britain
summary: Common belief about the fae courts and demons.

claims.text: Folk say the Unseelie Court shelters blood-drinkers, flesh-eaters, redcaps and warriors whose elfshot kills any human it touches, while the Seelie Court guards the innocent.
The Welsh fae, the Tylwyth Teg, are said to love horses and always to wear green, even in disguise.
In parts of Ireland the demon Cromm Cruach is still worshipped and appears as a living golden head.
